_note: Mars events. Each sol from schedule.firstSol there's a chance of one event, rising every sol (escalation). Every event pauses the game with a decision card. Numbers marked GAME are balance; realStory lines are real and fact-checked. {braces} are filled in by the game.

events.name: Dust storm
events.warning: Orbiters have spotted a dust storm heading your way. It arrives tomorrow and could last several sols.
events._numbers: GAME: a regional storm halves solar output (global storms like 2018's are far darker but rare). After it, panels stay 20% dusty and slowly clear (real wind gusts clean panels too).

choices.label: Switch off the greenhouses
choices.detail: Saves their power during the storm, but the crops die and have to regrow.

choices.label: Switch off the ice drills
choices.detail: Saves their power during the storm. The crew drinks from stored water.

choices.label: Ride it out
choices.detail: Keep everything on. If power runs short, the least important systems switch off by themselves.

events.realStory: In June 2018, a planet-wide dust storm blocked the Sun over NASA's Opportunity rover. Its solar panels couldn't recharge its batteries and it never woke up again. The nuclear-powered Curiosity rover kept working through the same storm.
events.science: Mars air is too thin for storms to blow a base over. The real danger is losing sunlight for days.
events.debrief: A dust storm on sols {from} to {to} cut your solar power to {pct}%.

events.name: Solar particle event
events.warning: Space weather forecasters have spotted a huge solar flare. A burst of radiation will reach Mars within hours.
events._numbers: GAME: 30 mSv for an unshielded crew in an average sector, scaled by the sector's radiation.

choices.label: Pile regolith on the habitat now
choices.detail: Costs {cost} regolith. Adds a permanent layer of shielding before the burst hits.

choices.label: Stay put and take the dose
choices.detail: Costs nothing now, but the crew's radiation dose goes up by about {dose} mSv.

events.realStory: During the huge 'Halloween' solar storms of 2003, astronauts on the International Space Station took shelter in the Zvezda module, one of the best-shielded parts of the station.
events.science: Solar storms are much easier to block than everyday cosmic rays. Rock, soil and water all make good shields.
events.debrief: A solar particle event on sol {sol} gave the crew {dose} mSv.

events.name: Equipment failure
events.warning: Alarm! Your {building} has broken down and stopped working.
events._numbers: GAME: repairing now costs 50% of the building's metal, slowly costs 20% and takes 2 sols.

choices.label: Repair it now
choices.detail: Costs {repairNow} metal. Working again straight away.

choices.label: Repair it slowly
choices.detail: Costs {repairSlow} metal. Working again in {slowSols} sols.

choices.label: Leave it for now
choices.detail: Free, but it stays broken. You can repair it later from its info card.

events.realStory: In 2004 the space station's main oxygen generator, Elektron, broke down several times. The crew kept breathing by burning 'oxygen candles' (each gives one person a day of oxygen) while they fixed it.
events.science: Machines break, especially far from home. Spare parts and a second machine (redundancy) keep crews alive.
